document.title: GE Combined-Cycle Product Line and Performance

paragraphs.text: Over about four decades, gas turbine designs grew to larger capacities (50 MW to 380 MW) with higher specific power, and efficient, economical combined-cycle systems were developed in step with them. GE names its pre-engineered combined-cycle line STAG™, short for STeam And Gas. Every STAG system is supplied as an Engineered Equipment Package (EEP) comprising GE gas turbines and steam turbines together with generators, controls and Heat Recovery Steam Generators (HRSGs). The highest-efficiency STAG configuration is built around the GE "H" model gas turbine, planned to enter commercial operation by 2003 and expected to reach 60 percent (LHV) thermal efficiency.

The EEP is described as an optimized, matched set of high-technology generating equipment, software and services, arranged for easy integration with balance of plant and auxiliaries provided by the owner. Since GE is the single source for the EEP, it is able to guarantee plant thermal and emission performance and to warrant system operation. The line covers both 50 and 60 Hz service, and its many configurations with standard options let each plant be fitted to its economic needs. It has two main categories: pre-engineered systems fired on oil or natural gas for producing electricity, and pre-engineered building blocks for combined-cycle cogeneration and for coal- or oil-fired integrated gasification combined-cycle (IGCC) plants. The authors identify economical performance as the defining trait of STAG systems; the contributing features are listed in Table 1 (power generation) and Table 2 (thermal energy and power systems).

Table 1. STAG combined-cycle power generation system features: Feature 1=High Thermal Efficiency; Feature 2=Low Installed Cost; Feature 3=Fuel Flexibility – Wide Range of Gas and Liquid Fuels; Feature 4=Low Operation and Maintenance Cost; Feature 5=Operating Flexibility – Base, Mid-range, Daily Start; Feature 6=High Reliability; Feature 7=High Availability; Feature 8=Short Installation Time; Feature 9=High Efficiency in Small Capacity Increments.

paragraphs.text: Table 3. STAG combined-cycle system designations (codes for single-shaft and multi-shaft configurations): S207FA-MS: S=STAG™; 2=Two GTs; 07FA=GT Model Series; MS=Multi-Shaft Configuration; diagram shows two GEN–GT–HRSG trains feeding one ST GEN. The table also notes that STAG stands for STeam And Gas.

The STAG line is offered in single-shaft and multi-shaft forms, illustrated with simplified block diagrams in Figure 1. A single-shaft unit consists of a gas turbine, a steam turbine, a generator and an HRSG, one of each, with the gas turbine and steam turbine driving the single generator in tandem on one shaft. A multi-shaft system uses one or more gas turbine generators, each with an HRSG, whose steam is collected in a common header and sent to one separate steam turbine generator.

Non-reheat steam cycles with one or several pressure levels are used with GE gas turbines whose rating point exhaust gas temperature is about 1000°F / 538°C or lower. Whether a single- or multiple-pressure cycle is chosen for a given plant depends on an economic evaluation that weighs installed plant cost, fuel cost and quality, plant-duty cycle, and O&M cost. Reheat steam cycles with multiple pressures are used with GE gas turbines whose rating point exhaust gas temperature is about 1100°F / 593°C or higher.

Figure 2 gives a generalized capability map of combined-cycle power output and thermal energy, representative of a plant delivering process steam at 150 psig/11.4 bars with a gas turbine of 100 MW rated output. On its vertical axis, where thermal energy is zero,, it shows power and thermal efficiency for unfired, supplementary-fired and fully-fired steam cycles. Unfired HRSGs built from modular pre-engineered components give the best power generation efficiency and also the lowest cost, which is why the STAG power generation line uses them. Supplementary-fired combined cycles are supplied for particular customers whose need for extra power outweighs the accompanying loss of thermal efficiency.

For cogeneration, Figure 2 indicates that fully-fired HRSGs give the highest efficiency at maximum thermal energy output. However, they are expensive because of water wall construction and the need to erect them in the field, and they can raise emission issues when plant siting requirements are assessed. The cogeneration region of main interest is therefore covered by unfired and supplementary-fired steam cycles, which span a thermal energy to electric power ratio of 0–12,000 Btu thermal energy per kW (0–12,660 kJ per kW); this range defines the cogeneration capability offered by the product line.
Figure 1 caption: STAG system configurations. Figure 2 caption: Generalized combined-cycle performance capability.

The power generation line offers several steam cycle choices so that each plant can match its fuels, fuel cost, duty cycle and other economic and operating requirements. The first is the Single-Pressure, Non-Reheat Heat Recovery Feedwater Heating cycle (Figure 3; HRSG schematic in Figure 4). Its unfired HRSG has finned tube superheater, evaporator and economizer sections, and heat is taken from the exhaust gas by convective heat transfer. As the simplest cycle usable in a combined cycle, it is widely applied and has low installed cost. It does not give the best combined-cycle efficiency, but it is a sensible choice when fuel is cheap, when the plant serves peaking duty, or when ash-bearing, high-sulfur fuel is burned. In the STAG line it is mainly paired with GE gas turbines whose baseload exhaust gas temperature is about 1000°F / 538°C or lower, and its HRSG stack gas temperature is roughly 340°F / 171°C.

In the Multiple-Pressure, Non-Reheat Heat Recovery / Feedwater Heating cycle, steam is raised at more than one pressure to recover as much gas turbine exhaust energy as possible. The gas-side and steam-side temperature profiles in Figures 5 and 6 (single-pressure versus multiple-pressure) show that adding pressure levels narrows the energy gap between the exhaust gas and the steam/water. Two- and three-pressure cycles are more efficient than single-pressure ones but cost more to install, so they pay off when fuel is expensive or the duty cycle demands a high load factor. The three-pressure cycle (Figure 7; HRSG schematic in Figure 8) resembles the single-pressure cycle with added low-pressure and intermediate-pressure sections. The performance gain comes from the extra heat transfer surface in the HRSG, and the stack gas temperature falls to between 200°F / 93°C and 260°F / 127°C.

The Three-Pressure, Reheat Heat Recovery Feedwater Heating cycle is matched to the "EC," "F," and "H" technology gas turbines. Their exhaust gas temperature of 1100°F / 593°C or more supplies enough high-temperature energy to the HRSG for reheat to be worthwhile. With the "EC" and "F" machines, the cycle also heats fuel gas to about 365°F / 185°C using water taken from the HRSG IP economizer discharge. The cycle diagram is Figure 9 and the HRSG schematic is Figure 10.

The "H" platform gas turbines, MS7001H and MS9001H, cool their hot gas path components with a closed-loop steam-cooling system combined with an open-loop air-cooling system. The reheat steam cycle used with them is tightly coupled to the gas turbine steam-cooling system, which gives a further reason to adopt the single-shaft STAG arrangement for these machines. The S107H and S109H steam cycle is shown in Figure 11 and the HRSG schematic in Figure 12. According to the authors, no power generation systems available at that time were more efficient than these STAG units.

The base configuration of the STAG power generation line targets high efficiency on natural gas or distillate fuel, and its equipment and system arrangement is summarized in Table 4. Ratings for the 60 Hz line are in Table 5 with the corresponding major equipment in Table 6; the 50 Hz ratings are in Table 7 and equipment in Table 8. All ratings assume gas turbine base load on natural gas fuel, while Table 9 defines nominal throttle and reheat steam conditions for both the non-reheat and reheat lines. The natural gas ratings of Tables 5 and 7 reflect the thermodynamic optimum, which is expected to coincide with the economic optimum for baseload and mid-range dispatch on clean fuels priced at about $2.50 per 10^6 Btu, HHV ($2.64 per 10^6 kJ, HHV).

Table 4. Beyond the base configuration, Table 10 lists the options most often applied. Non-reheat cycles with one or two pressures and reheat cycles with two pressures can also be supplied, with typical performance differences given in Table 11. HRSGs with forced circulation evaporators are offered for particular site conditions or owner preference; Figure 13 shows a two-pressure, non-reheat cycle with such an HRSG. A deaerator integral to the HRSG can be fitted, using low-pressure evaporator energy to deaerate feedwater at positive pressure for a small loss in thermal efficiency. Where a low-pressure economizer is included for high efficiency, corrosion-resistant material is needed, because the feedwater in that section may carry high oxygen and the outer tube surface may be colder than the exhaust gas dew point. Figure 14 shows a three-pressure non-reheat HRSG with integral deaerator.

Fuel properties influence combined-cycle performance in several ways. Hydrogen-rich fuels such as natural gas produce combustion products with much water, and because water carries more heat than air or the other combustion products, such fuels raise output and efficiency. Ash-bearing fuels foul both the gas turbine and the HRSG, so the design allowances needed to tolerate fouling lower plant output and efficiency. Fuel sulfur may require raising the stack gas temperature and the temperature of water entering the HRSG economizer so that corrosive sulfuric acid does not condense; the higher stack temperature that more sulfur demands reduces output and efficiency. Table 12 gives the performance change with fuel type, reflecting the typical hydrogen, ash and sulfur content of each.

Gas turbines in the STAG line can be fitted with Dry Low NOx (DLN) combustors that hold stack gas NOx down to 9 ppmvd at 15% oxygen (15.5 g/GJ) on natural gas without any water or steam injection. On distillate oil, water or steam injection may still be needed to satisfy NOx limits. Conventional diffusion flame combustors, run with water or steam injection to meet NOx limits, are also available. Table 13 lists stack gas NOx for gas turbines in typical STAG combined cycles burning natural gas with either DLN or diffusion flame combustors, and also shows the influence of water or steam injection on NOx reduction and thermal performance.

Selective catalytic reduction (SCR) lowers stack gas NOx by having ammonia react with NOx on a catalyst, converting it to nitrogen and water. SCR adds to installation and operating cost but can bring NOx below 9 ppmvd at 15% oxygen (15.5 g/GJ) for every combined-cycle system in the line. Because the SCR catalyst normally works between 570°F/300°C and 750°F/400°C, it is usually placed inside the high-pressure evaporator, as in Figure 15. The ammonia injection grid sits upstream of that evaporator, at a point where the gas is cooler than the temperature at which ammonia would oxidize to NOx, so ammonia and NOx mix thoroughly while flowing through the pre-evaporator section.

Carbon monoxide (CO) emissions stay low when gas turbine load exceeds 50%, typically below 5–25 ppmvd (9-43 g/GJ), owing to very efficient combustion. If lower CO is required, catalytic CO abatement can be added; the CO catalyst is placed in the exhaust gas path, normally upstream of the HRSG superheater. For raising combined-cycle plant output, the available options are compressor inlet cooling, power augmentation by steam or water injection, HRSG supplementary firing, and gas turbine peak load capability, used chiefly to add capacity during peak periods.

Evaporative compressor inlet cooling is an effective way to add capacity where ambient air is hot and dry. A cooler of 85% effectiveness is expected to lift plant output by about 5% at site conditions of 90°F / 32°C and 30% relative humidity. Evaporative and mechanical chiller systems can bring gas turbine inlet air down to as low as 45°F / 7°C, giving up to 11% more capacity at 90°F / 32°C and 30% relative humidity. Neither evaporative cooling nor chilling raises combined-cycle plant efficiency, but either can be an economic source of extra peak power in warm summer periods.

HRSG supplementary firing can raise steam turbine capability by up to 100%, which adds about 25% to plant capacity. It is usually justified by cogeneration of power and process energy, though peaking capacity credits or evening out fuel use across the ambient temperature range to suit "take-or-pay" fuel contracts can also warrant it. Power produced by supplemental firing has an incremental efficiency of 34–36%, on the fuel's lower heating value. Gas turbine water or steam injection can boost output as well as lower NOx, but it worsens plant efficiency. Gas turbine peak load capability, offered on many configurations, can add 3–10% combined-cycle capacity; it may be the cheapest route to small, short-duration capacity additions, since running at peak load markedly shortens gas turbine parts life and raises maintenance cost. Table 14 gives a summary of how these enhancement options affect performance.

Combining combined-cycle plants with gasification yields efficient coal- or oil-fired plants with strong environmental performance, and the standard STAG modules can easily be adapted for integrated gasification combined cycles (IGCCs). Figure 16 depicts an advanced "H" platform IGCC with an oxygen-blown gasifier and an air separation unit integrated with the gas turbine. The authors expect this system to generate power economically on fuels such as coal, petroleum coke and heavy residual oil, as well as other solid or low-grade liquid fuels. Its ratings are given as ranges because they depend on gasifier type, gas clean-up systems, air and steam cycle integration, the analysis of the coal or other fuel, and fuel moisture content.

The principal equipment of STAG combined-cycle power generation plants is made up of packaged gas turbine generating units, steam turbine-generators, unfired HRSGs and controls. The authors describe this as a proven, reliable equipment line with very good performance for combined-cycle use. GE builds the gas turbine generators and steam turbine generators, while HRSGs and controls are selected so that every application forms a coordinated combined-cycle system. The sections that follow describe the equipment features that matter most for efficient, reliable combined cycles.

The GE gas turbines used in STAG plants and their ratings are listed in Table 15. Figure 17 gives a cross-section of the PG7121EA, representative of GE gas turbines with a 2035°F / 1113°C firing temperature, while the PG9171E fires at 2055°F / 1124°C. Figure 18 is a cross-section of the PG9351FA, representative of the 2420°F / 1327°C firing-temperature machines, PG7241FA among them. The next-generation "FB" and "H" platforms were anticipated to begin commercial operation during the early part of the 2000s decade, per the paper. The "H" machine (cross-section in Figure 19) has a four-stage turbine whose stages one and two are cooled by closed-loop steam cooling, and, to get the best performance at a 2600°F / 1426°C firing temperature, its compressor has a raised pressure ratio and is derived from the GE CF680C2 aircraft engine.

The gas turbine property with the greatest influence on combined-cycle performance is specific power, meaning the gas turbine's power divided by its airflow, expressed as kW output per lb/sec of compressor airflow. As Figure 20 shows, combined-cycle thermal efficiency increases with gas turbine specific power, and firing temperature is the main factor setting specific power. Gains in combined-cycle efficiency have therefore come mostly from higher firing temperatures, made possible by high-temperature / high strength materials, corrosion-resistant coatings and better cooling technology; combined-cycle development and efficiency have advanced alongside gas turbine technology.

STAG systems using "F" technology gas turbines reach net thermal efficiencies of 53% (LHV) or more, and those using "H" technology reach 58–60% (LHV); the respective rated firing temperatures are 2420°F / 1327°C and 2600°F / 1426°C. The "FA" turbine has a 15.5 pressure ratio and the "H" turbine a 23.0 pressure ratio, giving the highest specific power for their firing temperatures, which yields the lowest simple-cycle installed cost together with high combined-cycle efficiency. An exhaust gas temperature band of 1000–1100°F / 538–566°C is especially suitable for combined cycles, since heat moves from exhaust gas to the steam cycle across a small temperature difference, maximizing thermodynamic availability with the hottest, most efficient steam cycles.

Multiple can-annular combustors using film and impingement cooling meet environmental requirements worldwide and operate dependably at high firing temperatures across fuels ranging from natural gas up to residual oil. The chosen materials, coatings and cooling arrangements permit reliable high-firing-temperature operation, which gives high specific power and high combined-cycle efficiency. Most current GE gas turbines cool the hot gas path in an open loop, largely by film cooling with compressor air. This produces a substantial temperature drop across the first stage nozzle and requires a large amount of "chargeable air" to cool the turbine stages; both the nozzle temperature drop and the chargeable cooling losses grow as turbine inlet temperature rises.

The advanced "H" platform instead uses an integrated closed-loop steam-cooling system. Dropping film cooling in favor of closed-loop steam cooling lets turbine inlet temperature rise without a higher combustion temperature, since the first stage nozzle temperature drop is greatly reduced (Figure 21); NOx can thus remain low even at the higher inlet temperature. The system also removes the need for "chargeable cooling air" for the stationary and rotating airfoils of stages one and two, which improves combined cycle thermal efficiency by two percentage points.

Factory packaging and containerized shipping of small parts keep installed cost low and installation short. Reliability is credited to step-by-step design evolution of parts, quality-focused manufacturing that includes running factory tests on the gas turbine and its accessories, follow-up support from experienced installation and service staff, and good spare parts support. Maintenance costs are low thanks to these features plus a design that allows easy access, including borescope ports for inspecting key parts without dismantling. Through its accessory systems, combustion systems and turbine components, the heavy-duty line can burn a wide range of fuels: 150-400 Btu/scf (6520-16,850 kJ/nm^3) gaseous fuels, including those derived from coal, coke or heavy petroleum products, and liquid fuels such as naphtha, light distillates, heavy distillates, crude oil and residual oil.

STAG HRSGs are unfired and of modular construction, with finned-tube heat transfer surface and either natural- or forced-circulation evaporators. Figure 22 shows a modular natural circulation HRSG, and Figure 23 an installation of two such units serving MS7001EA gas turbines; Figure 24 shows the modular forced-circulation type and Figure 25 an installation of it in a STAG 107EA plant. Normally each gas turbine has its own HRSG. In STAG plants with the MS6001B gas turbine, however, the standard ducting routes the exhaust of two gas turbines into one HRSG, although one HRSG per gas turbine can also be supplied. The HRSG and its auxiliaries are designed around the specific operating needs of the STAG combined cycle.

Listed HRSG design features: an exhaust gas bypass system that enables fast startup and shutdown and operating flexibility in multi-shaft STAG plants (single-shaft units do not use exhaust gas bypass); a flexible tube support system for fast startup and load following; low gas side pressure drop to optimize gas turbine performance; large factory-tested modules that ship ready for short installation time and low construction cost; and fuel flexibility, meaning reliable, efficient operation on exhaust from gas turbines burning anything from natural gas to residual oil.

Figure 22 caption: Modular construction of a natural-circulation HRSG. Figure 23 caption: Two natural-circulation HRSGs operating with MS7001EA gas turbines. Figure 24 caption: Modular construction of a forced-circulation HRSG. Figure 25 caption: Forced-circulation HRSG with PG7111EA gas turbines.

GE supplies a full range of steam turbines for combined cycles, with at least two choices for every STAG offering. Turbines with different exhaust annulus areas allow optimization for site condenser cooling conditions. A large exhaust annulus costs more but increases capability and can be the best value where steam turbine exhaust pressure is low; where exhaust pressure is high, a small-annulus turbine gives equal or greater capability at lower cost and is the economic choice. Figure 26 compares four last-stage buckets available for the STAG 107FA. Across the STAG line, last-stage bucket lengths span 14.3 inches / 363 mm up to 42 inches / 1067 mm.

With no extractions for feedwater heating and steam admitted at three pressures, exhaust flow is roughly 30% higher than throttle flow. The last stage can produce up to 15% of steam turbine output, so last-stage efficiency and exhaust annulus sizing matter greatly in combined cycles. Like all current GE last-stage buckets, these use a continuously-coupled design for efficiency and reliability, which allows many fairly slender blades with narrow, tightly controlled flow passages, especially at the high-velocity tip. Covers cut tip leakage losses, add damping and help keep the flow passage under control.

Designs for high exhaust pressure, as needed with air-cooled condensers at high ambient temperature, are offered and can operate dependably and efficiently with exhaust pressure as high as 15 inches Hg,a/381mm Hg,a. For steam turbines above 80 MW, advanced 3D aero packages combining advanced vortex design, contoured sidewalls in the inlet section and added radial tip spill strips help maximize combined cycle efficiency. The line includes axial exhaust and down exhaust arrangements; axial exhaust is favored for single-flow turbines, usually in small STAG plants (Figure 27). Reheat steam turbines designed for combined cycles are offered for "EC," "F," and "H" plants. The single-shaft STAG 107FA, STAG 109FA and STAG 109H are integrated machines with a solid turbine/generator coupling and a single-thrust bearing, sharing lubrication, hydraulic and control systems between gas and steam turbine. Figure 28 shows a two-flow reheat steam turbine.

Features of steam turbines designed for combined-cycle duty: shippable assembled modules with a low profile installation that cuts installation time and cost (and building cost for indoor plants); borescopic inspection of nozzles and buckets possible with the upper casing left in place; quick starting and load following enabled by a shaft kept to minimum diameter around the first stage, generous fillets where the wheels join the rotor, long coupling spans, vertical flexible plate support near the centerline with keys to maintain alignment, and off-shell valves with full-arc steam admission; main steam, cold reheat and hot reheat pipes all attached to the lower half of the shell, easing upper-half removal for maintenance and avoiding bolted joints in high temperature piping; and sliding pressure operation with control valves wide open, so no inlet control stage is needed. At 1800 psig/124 bar,g, the high-pressure stages and reheat inlet use single wall construction; at 2400 psig/165 bar,g, a short inner shell surrounds the early high-pressure stages, lowering the load on horizontal joint bolting and the shell flange thickness.
Figure 26 caption: STAG steam turbine last-stage bucket selection. Figure 27 caption: Non-reheat, single casing, axial exhaust steam turbine. Figure 28 caption: Two-flow, reheat steam turbine.

Generators for STAG gas and steam turbines are assembled and tested in the factory. Smaller STAG plants built around PG6581B, PG6101FA and PG7121EA gas turbines use air-cooled generators as standard, which may be open-ventilated or of the totally enclosed water-to-air cooled type. When open-ventilated, they are fitted with self-cleaning air filters suited to deserts and other dusty or dirty locations (Figure 29). Single-shaft and larger multi-shaft STAG plants use hydrogen-cooled generators as standard, cooled either by plant cooling water or by ambient air through water-to-air heat exchangers; a typical packaged hydrogen-cooled generator for a gas turbine appears in Figure 30.
Figure 29 caption: Air-cooled generator with a self-cleaning air filter. Figure 30 caption: Typical packaged hydrogen-cooled generator.

Plant control uses a distributed digital control system whose data highway is redundant, and the station operator consoles give interactive color graphic views of the whole plant in enough detail for convenient operation. Multi-shaft and single-shaft control systems share the same core aims: simplicity, easy starting, automated operation and very good load following. Each main plant component has its own control panel and interface, which pass information and commands to and from the operator via data highways to the console, whose detailed graphics allow informative interaction with the plant.

In the single-shaft case, the power train is an uncomplicated tandem layout without an exhaust bypass system, rigidly coupled to one generator with a shared overspeed protection device and fewer auxiliaries; Figures 31 and 32 give block diagrams for multi-shaft and single-shaft plants. The heat recovery combined cycle needs few control loops, as the control diagram for a single-pressure, multi-shaft STAG plant shows (Figure 33). This simplicity, combined with well-proven automatic operation of individual components, allows the entire plant to be automated and keeps control room staffing small; most STAG plants run with one control room operator plus one roving operator.

Multi-shaft STAG control supports automated startup and operation once plant auxiliaries are started by remote manual action, remote manual control of the individual major components, or running the gas turbine-generators from local control compartments. This arrangement maximizes availability, because remote operation needs no additional control room operators. Equipment protection resides in the unit controls, so normal protection stays active in every operating mode, local or remote manual operation included.

Each single-shaft unit has a microprocessor-based controller that coordinates its own components and exchanges information with the plant-level control. With a simple steam cycle, gas and steam turbines coupled in tandem to one generator, and no HRSG exhaust-gas bypass system, this control is very simple, and starting, operation and shutdown of each unit are automatic. A local unit control system links to the central control room console through a data highway, letting one control room operator, helped by one local operator, run one or more single-shaft units.

Figure 31 caption: Distributed control system for a plant with multi-shaft STAG combined cycle. Figure 32 caption: Distributed control system for a plant with single-shaft STAG combined cycle. Figure 33 caption: Multi-shaft STAG control diagram.

STAG ratings assume a once-through condenser cooling system using seawater or river water. Configurations can also be built with many owner-specified auxiliaries, such as evaporative cooling towers and air-cooled condensers. With these alternatives, plant capability and efficiency are expected to be lower, since steam turbine exhaust pressure and the power drawn by cooling system auxiliaries both increase.

Figure 34 presents ambient-temperature effect curves for heat rate and output capability, illustrating how a typical STAG plant varies with ambient air temperature. Heat rate stays low across the whole ambient range, and the low heat rate and rising output at lower ambient temperature result from gas turbine characteristics and optimal equipment matching. Gas turbine exhaust flow and temperature change with ambient temperature and barometric pressure, and steam production and steam turbine output follow the exhaust flow and temperature delivered to the HRSG. Steam turbines are chosen for each application, and in the standard systems they are sized so their rated flow equals the steam production.

Very good part-load heat rate is obtained on multi-shaft plants or groups of single-shaft units by loading gas turbines one after another to meet demand (Figure 35). The same curve shows the plant can follow load efficiently with all gas turbines running, heat rate rising only 1% at about 80% of rating. Modulated inlet guide vanes (IGV) on the compressor are a major contributor: they regulate airflow between the "hash mark" and point "B", holding firing temperature almost constant so cycle thermodynamic quality is essentially unchanged; stack and condenser losses scale roughly with output, keeping heat rate nearly flat. Below the hash mark, airflow is held constant and firing temperature drops as load falls.

STAG plants start and load quickly, suiting them to mid-range and daily start peaking duty as well as baseload. Full load is typically reached within one hour on a hot start and in about three hours on a cold start. In multi-shaft plants the gas turbines can start independently of the steam cycle, reaching about 65% of plant capability in 15–25 minutes (the time depends on gas turbine size) for hot, warm and cold starts (Figure 36). Single-shaft plants reach full capacity in roughly the same time, but their startup sequence and load profile differ because gas and steam turbines start as one integrated unit rather than two; see Figure 37.

Figure 34 caption: Combined-cycle ambient air temperature effect curve. Figure 35 caption: STAG 200 part-load performance. Figure 36 caption: Multi-shaft STAG starting times. Figure 37 caption: Single-shaft STAG starting times.

STAG equipment can be fitted to the installation needs set by different climates, system configurations and owner/operator preferences, and is suited to outdoor, semi-outdoor or fully enclosed plants; arrangements have been developed for every STAG system. Plan views cover the multi-shaft S406B (Figure 38), multi-shaft S207EA (Figure 39), single-shaft S109E (Figure 40), multi-shaft S207FA (Figure 41) and single-shaft S107FA (Figure 42), with an elevation of the single-shaft S107FA in Figure 43. Figure 44 gives S107H and S109H plan and elevation views; the S107H delivers about 58% more combined-cycle output with only about 10% more footprint area.

Further examples: Figure 45 shows a 220 MW STAG 207E installation, Figure 46 a STAG 109FA plant, and Figure 47 a 4000 MW site with eight STAG 107F and four STAG 207FA systems, which uses indoor turbine-generator equipment with outdoor HRSGs. Figure 48 shows a plant housing two STAG multi-shaft units indoors. For outdoor plants, the standard gas turbine enclosures are built weatherproof, and steam turbines can be given weatherproof lagging for the steam turbines.

STAG plants are economical partly because they install quickly and cheaply, because every major component is factory packaged and small parts travel in containers (containerized shipping). Beyond lower direct construction cost, the short schedule cuts interest paid during construction, and standard factory modules and designs reduce plant engineering time and cost. For pre-engineered, standardized STAG designs, order to commercial operation typically takes 24 months, excluding permitting. Multi-shaft plants can be built in two phases to shorten the time to first power: the gas turbines supply 65% of plant capacity and can usually be installed in under 18 months, generating while the steam system is completed. Figure 49 gives a typical two-phase multi-shaft schedule.
Figure 49 caption: Typical multi-shaft combined-cycle project schedule.

Adding generating capacity in small steps as utility load grows can improve power generation economics, and STAG plants suit this because efficient, low-cost units come in small capacity blocks. The pro-generation approach adds further flexibility: simple-cycle gas turbine plants initially fired on natural gas/distillate oil can later be converted to combined cycle as demand rises. When first committing to simple-cycle gas turbines, the main points to plan for are the plot plan area reserved for later steam cycle equipment and the capability of the transmission line. Later conversion to coal-derived fuels is another way to hedge long-term uncertainty in conventional fuel availability and price.

paragraphs.section: Thermal Energy and Power System Product Line
paragraphs.text: The thermal energy and power line (cogeneration and district heating combined cycles) is built with structured flexibility to cover a broad span of power and thermal capacities. The most commonly supplied systems are: (1) steam generation at process conditions with an HRSG and no steam turbine, using an unfired or supplemental-fired HRSG; (2) an HRSG with a non-condensing steam turbine exhausting to process, using an unfired one-pressure, unfired two-pressure, or supplemental-fired one-pressure HRSG; and (3) an HRSG with an extraction/condensing steam turbine, with the same three HRSG choices.

paragraphs.section: Thermal Energy and Power System Product Line
paragraphs.text: Capabilities of these systems are specific to each gas turbine frame size and each set of process steam conditions, both for unfired process HRSGs and for unfired HRSGs paired with non-condensing steam turbines. Systems combining fired HRSGs with condensing steam turbines offer very wide flexibility in thermal energy and power capacity for every frame size. The performance parameters reported are net plant power, LHV heat content of the fuel consumed, thermal energy in steam sent to process, thermal efficiency, and fuel charged to power (FCP).

paragraphs.section: Thermal Energy and Power System Product Line
paragraphs.text: Thermal efficiency equation: η_TH = 100 x (Q_p + Q_TE) / Q_F (thermal efficiency = 100 × (net power output + process steam thermal energy) ÷ fuel LHV heat input). Symbols: η_TH = thermal efficiency - LHV (%); Q_F = LHV heat content of fuel consumption (Btu/hr, kJ/hr); Q_p = net power output (Btu/hr, kJ/hr); Q_TE = thermal energy in process steam (Btu/hr, kJ/hr).

paragraphs.section: Thermal Energy and Power System Product Line
paragraphs.text: Fuel charged to power (FCP) is used to compare an integrated thermal energy and power plant against separate facilities producing the same power and thermal energy. To obtain it, the LHV fuel heat that a conventional fired boiler would need to make the same thermal energy is deducted from the integrated system's LHV heat consumption. The resulting FCP is then set against the heat rate of a stand-alone power generation plant, which indicates how the integrated system performs relative to separate thermal energy and power generation.
terms: integrated thermal energy and power plant

paragraphs.section: Thermal Energy and Power System Product Line
paragraphs.text: FCP equation as printed: FCP = 100 x (Q_p - [Q_TE/η_B]) / p (fuel charged to power = integrated-system fuel heat minus the fuel a fired boiler would need for the same process heat, per unit of net electrical output). Symbols: FCP = fuel charged to power = LHV (Btu/kWH, kJ/hr); Q_F = LHV heat content of fuel consumption (Btu/hr, kJ/hr); Q_TE = thermal energy in process steam (Btu/hr, kJ/hr); η_B = LHV efficiency of fired boiler producing equivalent thermal energy (%); P = net electrical output (kW).

paragraphs.section: Thermal Energy and Power System Product Line
paragraphs.text: Figure 50 presents cycle diagrams of thermal energy and power combined cycles producing steam at process conditions, using either an unfired or a supplementary-fired HRSG; an HRSG designed for supplementary firing gives the largest process steam energy supply. Figure 51 covers cogeneration combined cycles equipped with non-condensing steam turbines. Many variants can meet particular process energy needs, such as single automatic-extraction steam turbines supplying steam efficiently at two or three pressures, and multi-pressure HRSGs delivering steam at several pressure and temperature conditions. Extraction condensing steam turbines give the greatest flexibility; Figure 52 shows typical single automatic extraction systems, which can run at reduced process steam demand and use surplus steam for power in the condensing section. Systems may also be supplied with double automatic extraction turbines combined with HRSGs of multiple pressures for specific process steam requirements.

Figure 52 caption: Cycle diagrams – thermal energy and power combined cycle with extraction/condensing steam turbines.

GE's Combined-Cycle Engineered Equipment Package (EEP) bundles equipment and services in a distinctive way. The owner receives a plant performance guarantee and operating warranty, plus service capability covering the whole power generation system, while still allowing the plant design, auxiliaries and structures to be customized. This is accomplished by putting in GE's scope the major combined-cycle equipment that must be closely coordinated to ensure performance and operating objectives are met. Table 16 shows how equipment scope is divided between GE and the owner, and Table 17 the division of services and software. The key items in GE's EEP scope are the combined-cycle system design and interface definition, which allow the owner, or the owner's architect-engineer or engineer-constructor, to design the plant for project-specific requirements.

Table 16. Equipment scope split with engineered equipment package. General Electric scope=Gas Turbine(s); Steam Turbine(s); Generator(s); Heat Recovery Steam Generator(s); Plant Controls. Owner scope=Mechanical Auxiliaries; Electrical Auxiliaries; Main Electrical Connections; Balance of Plant (Foundations and Structures; Switchyard; Fuel Handling and Storage; Plant Cooling System; Construction Materials; Site Preparation Materials).

Table 17. Services and software split with engineered equipment package. General Electric scope=Plant performance and environmental guarantee; Combined cycle system design and warranty; Balance of plant equipment functional specifications; Equipment interface drawings; Steady state and dynamic interface definition; Equipment operation and maintenance; Operation and maintenance training; Construction and operation permit support; Performance and environmental test support. Owner scope=Construction and operation permits; Plant design; Plant construction; Plant start-up, commissioning and operation; Performance and environmental testing; Site preparation; Project administration.

The authors conclude that the STAG combined-cycle line, spanning 60 MW to 750 MW and including both power generation systems and thermal energy and power systems, offers efficient, low-cost plants that satisfy environmental requirements in every country. The GE combined cycle EEP assures that performance and operating objectives are met while still permitting a customized plant reflecting the owner's practices and preferences. Given their favorable economics, reliability and operating flexibility, the authors recommend considering these systems for all power generation applications.
